newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: U.S. to honor Nicaragua vote results, Carter says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to honor Nicaragua vote results, Carter says.

text.p: Former U.S. President Jimmy Carter, in Nicaragua to observe its Sunday presidential elections, said on Friday the U.S. government would respect the vote's results independent of which candidate won.
Earlier this month, a U.S. State Department spokesman questioned the democratic credentials of one of the top candidates, former President Daniel Ortega, an old U.S. nemesis.

We "have inquired at the highest levels in the State Department, and they've made it clear they do not express a preference for any candidate or party in the election, and the election's results will be accepted if they are judged to be fair and free," Carter told a news conference.
Carter was accompanied by former Secretary of State James Baker, who also will serve as an election observer.
Nicaragua's presidential vote has turned into a two-man race with right-wing Arnoldo Aleman of the Liberal Alliance narrowly leading Ortega of the left-wing Sandinista Front in public-opinion polls.
They are followed by a jumble of 21 lesser candidates.

The most recent CID-Gallup poll gave Aleman 40.5 percent of the vote and Ortega 37.9 percent. If no candidate gets 45 percent of the vote, a runoff will be held for the two top vote-getters in late November or early December.
Carter's comments came after a U.S. State Department spokesman said he "would not use the word democrat to describe Daniel Ortega" and told reporters: "We remember the past."

Dubbed a dictator by then-U.S. President Ronald Reagan, Ortega and his 1979 Sandinista revolution sparked massive U.S. intervention in Central America in the 1980s to counter what Washington saw as the threat of a Marxist domino effect across poverty-stricken countries in the region.
Ortega's Sandinistas fought an eight-year civil war against U.S.-armed Contra rebels in the 1980s that left 25,000 dead.
